The spherical cloak has an inner radius R1 and outer radius R2 with anisotropic permittivity and permeability tensors.
The cloak layer permittivity and permeability satisfy ǫt/ǫ0 = µt/µ0 = R2/(R2 - R1) and ǫr/ǫt = µr/µt = ((r - R1)^2)/r^2.
A time-harmonic electric dipole is placed inside the concealed region (r < R1) as an active source.
The electromagnetic fields are decomposed into TE and TM modes using scalar potentials ΨTE and ΨTM.
Boundary conditions enforce continuity of tangential electric and magnetic fields at r = R1 and r = R2.
The reflection coefficient RTM at the inner boundary is RTM = ζn(k1 R1) / ψn(k1 R1), where ζn and ψn are Riccati-Bessel functions.
No electromagnetic fields exist in the cloak layer (R1 < r < R2) or outside (r > R2) when an active source is inside.
The tangential electric field is discontinuous at the inner boundary due to induced surface electric voltage VE.
The cloak's inner boundary behaves like a perfect magnetic conductor (PMC) for TM waves and a perfect electric conductor (PEC) for TE waves.
The reflected wave from the inner boundary preserves the polarization handedness and phase, unlike reflection from PEC or PMC surfaces.
The induced electric and magnetic surface voltages correspond exactly to auxiliary scalar potentials ϕe and ϕm at the inner boundary.
Inside the concealed region, fields form standing waves with zero time-averaged Poynting power, indicating no net energy flow.
Surface voltages arise from zero radial permittivity and permeability at the inner boundary, causing infinite polarization.
As frequency ω approaches zero, electric surface voltage VE vanishes for static electric dipoles, while magnetic surface voltage VH remains.
The cloak can also cloak static magnetic fields, realizable with superconducting inner boundaries.
The surface voltages are not caused by conductive charges but by a distribution of polarized dipole moments on the interface.
The cloak's inner boundary acts as a special mirror that reflects waves without changing their polarization or phase information.
The mathematical auxiliary scalar potentials gain direct physical meaning as surface voltages in this cloaking scenario.
The cloak design is based on coordinate transformation methods first proposed by Pendry et al. in 2006.
The study confirms that a 'true' cloak must cloak active devices by preventing waves from escaping the concealed region.
